1. Project Instructions & Prerequisites¶

Project Instructions¶

Context: EHR data is becoming a key source of real-world evidence (RWE) for the pharmaceutical industry and regulators to make decisions on clinical trials. You are a data scientist for an exciting unicorn healthcare startup that has created a groundbreaking diabetes drug that is ready for clinical trial testing. It is a very unique and sensitive drug that requires administering the drug over at least 5-7 days of time in the hospital with frequent monitoring/testing and patient medication adherence training with a mobile application. You have been provided a patient dataset from a client partner and are tasked with building a predictive model that can identify which type of patients the company should focus their efforts testing this drug on. Target patients are people that are likely to be in the hospital for this duration of time and will not incur significant additional costs for administering this drug to the patient and monitoring.

In order to achieve your goal you must build a regression model that can predict the estimated hospitalization time for a patient and use this to select/filter patients for your study.

Expected Hospitalization Time Regression Model: Utilizing a synthetic dataset(denormalized at the line level augmentation) built off of the UCI Diabetes readmission dataset, students will build a regression model that predicts the expected days of hospitalization time and then convert this to a binary prediction of whether to include or exclude that patient from the clinical trial.

This project will demonstrate the importance of building the right data representation at the encounter level, with appropriate filtering and preprocessing/feature engineering of key medical code sets. This project will also require students to analyze and interpret their model for biases across key demographic groups.

Please see the project rubric online for more details on the areas your project will be evaluated.

Dataset¶

Due to healthcare PHI regulations (HIPAA, HITECH), there are limited number of publicly available datasets and some datasets require training and approval. So, for the purpose of this exercise, we are using a dataset from UC Irvine(https://archive.ics.uci.edu/ml/datasets/Diabetes+130-US+hospitals+for+years+1999-2008) that has been modified for this course. Please note that it is limited in its representation of some key features such as diagnosis codes which are usually an unordered list in 835s/837s (the HL7 standard interchange formats used for claims and remits).

Data Schema The dataset reference information can be https://github.com/udacity/nd320-c1-emr-data-starter/blob/master/project/data_schema_references/ . There are two CSVs that provide more details on the fields and some of the mapped values.

Project Submission¶

When submitting this project, make sure to run all the cells before saving the notebook. Save the notebook file as "student_project_submission.ipynb" and save another copy as an HTML file by clicking "File" -> "Download as.."->"html". Include the "utils.py" and "student_utils.py" files in your submission. The student_utils.py should be where you put most of your code that you write and the summary and text explanations should be written inline in the notebook. Once you download these files, compress them into one zip file for submission.

  • Intermediate level knowledge of Python
  • Basic knowledge of probability and statistics
  • Basic knowledge of machine learning concepts
  • Installation of Tensorflow 2.0 and other dependencies(conda environment.yml or virtualenv requirements.txt file provided)

Environment Setup¶

For step by step instructions on creating your environment, please go to https://github.com/udacity/nd320-c1-emr-data-starter/blob/master/project/README.md.

2. Learning Objectives¶

By the end of the project, you will be able to

  • Use the Tensorflow Dataset API to scalably extract, transform, and load datasets and build datasets aggregated at the line, encounter, and patient data levels(longitudinal)
  • Analyze EHR datasets to check for common issues (data leakage, statistical properties, missing values, high cardinality) by performing exploratory data analysis.
  • Create categorical features from Key Industry Code Sets (ICD, CPT, NDC) and reduce dimensionality for high cardinality features by using embeddings
  • Create derived features(bucketing, cross-features, embeddings) utilizing Tensorflow feature columns on both continuous and categorical input features
  • SWBAT use the Tensorflow Probability library to train a model that provides uncertainty range predictions that allow for risk adjustment/prioritization and triaging of predictions
  • Analyze and determine biases for a model for key demographic groups by evaluating performance metrics across groups by using the Aequitas framework

Determine Level of Dataset (Line or Encounter)¶

Question 1: Based off of analysis of the data, what level is this dataset? Is it at the line or encounter level? Are there any key fields besides the encounter_id and patient_nbr fields that we should use to aggregate on? Knowing this information will help inform us what level of aggregation is necessary for future steps and is a step that is often overlooked.

Student Response: The dataset is at the line level, not the encounter level. It has 143,424 rows but only 101,766 distinct encounter_ids (1.41 lines per encounter, at most 6) and 71,518 distinct patients. The evidence cell above shows that the only column whose value changes between the lines of one encounter is ndc_code: the file is denormalized so that an encounter is repeated once for every drug (NDC code) that was prescribed.

Besides encounter_id and patient_nbr the key field to handle is therefore ndc_code (after Question 3: generic_drug_name). It is the line-level field that must be aggregated: all other columns are grouped on (they are constant within an encounter) and the drug names of the encounter's lines are collected into one list that is turned into drug indicator columns. A second level exists above the encounter: a patient has 1.42 encounters on average (up to 40), so to avoid leakage between a patient's encounters the data must also be reduced to one encounter per patient (Question 4) and later split by patient_nbr (Question 6). The target time_in_hospital is an encounter-level quantity, so the final modeling table has one row per encounter (= one per patient).

In [5]:

Exploratory Data Analysis (Question 2)¶

The file is at the line level (see Question 1): the same encounter is repeated once for every NDC code. To describe a patient or an encounter field (age, gender, lab counts...) we therefore first reduce to one row per encounter (or per patient), otherwise encounters with many drugs would be counted several times.

In [6]:
numeric_fields = ['time_in_hospital', 'num_lab_procedures', 'num_medications', 'number_diagnoses',
                  'num_procedures', 'number_outpatient', 'number_inpatient', 'number_emergency']
enc_df = df.drop_duplicates('encounter_id').copy()      # one row per encounter
pat_df = df.drop_duplicates('patient_nbr').copy()       # one row per patient (used for demographics)

def pct_missing(s):
    # missing is stored as a real NaN, the placeholder '?', or 'None' (= lab test not measured, see the schema)
    return (s.isna() | s.astype(str).str.strip().isin(['?', '', 'None'])).mean() * 100

summary = pd.DataFrame({
    'pct_missing': enc_df.drop(columns=['encounter_id', 'patient_nbr']).apply(pct_missing),
})
summary['pct_zero'] = [(enc_df[c] == 0).mean() * 100 if c in numeric_fields else np.nan for c in summary.index]
summary['n_unique'] = df[summary.index].nunique()   # cardinality is read from the full line-level file
summary.sort_values('pct_missing', ascending=False).round(1)

Choosing the length-of-stay cutoff for patient selection¶

The drug needs at least 5-7 days in hospital, so the regression output (expected days) has to be turned into include/exclude with a cutoff of X days. The cutoff should come from the distribution of time_in_hospital:

In [11]:
los = enc_df['time_in_hospital']
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(15, 4.5))
los.value_counts().sort_index().plot(kind='bar', ax=axes[0], color=['#c0392b' if d >= 5 else '#7f8c8d' for d in sorted(los.unique())])
axes[0].set_title('time_in_hospital (encounters) - red = 5 days or more'); axes[0].set_xlabel('days'); axes[0].set_ylabel('encounters')
cum = pd.Series({d: (los >= d).mean() * 100 for d in range(1, 15)})
cum.plot(ax=axes[1], marker='o'); axes[1].set_title('% of encounters lasting AT LEAST d days'); axes[1].set_xlabel('d (days)'); axes[1].set_ylabel('%')
for d in (5, 7):
    axes[1].axvline(d, ls='--', c='r' if d == 5 else 'orange'); axes[1].annotate(f"{cum[d]:.0f}%", (d, cum[d]), textcoords='offset points', xytext=(6, 6))
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
print(los.describe().round(2).to_dict())
print({f">={d} days": f"{(los >= d).mean() * 100:.1f}%" for d in range(3, 9)})

Student Response: (all percentages are per encounter, i.e. after removing the line-level duplication; figures and tables are in the cells above)

a. Missing / zero values

  • Missing or "not measured": weight (96.9%), max_glu_serum (94.7% "None" = test not performed), A1Cresult (83.3% "None"), medical_specialty (49.1% "?"), payer_code (39.6% "?"), ndc_code (23.1% of encounters have no drug recorded) and, to a small extent, race (2.2% "?").
  • Zero values: number_emergency (88.8%), number_outpatient (83.6%), number_inpatient (66.5%) and num_procedures (45.8%). For these counts zero is a real value (no prior visits / no procedures), but the fields are dominated by it.

b. Gaussian shape - Only num_lab_procedures has an (approximately) Gaussian histogram: it is symmetric around ~43-44 tests (skew -0.24, excess kurtosis -0.25), apart from an extra spike at 1 test. num_medications is bell-shaped but clearly right-skewed (skew 1.33, heavy tail), time_in_hospital and num_procedures are right-skewed, number_diagnoses is left-skewed with a large spike at 9 (the value looks capped), and the three prior-visit counts are extremely skewed (almost all zeros).

c. High cardinality - other_diagnosis_codes (19,374 distinct values), primary_diagnosis_code (717), ndc_code (251) and medical_specialty (73) (the two IDs encounter_id/patient_nbr are identifiers, not features).

  • other_diagnosis_codes holds a pair of ICD-9 codes in one string ("250.01|255"), so the cardinality is the number of combinations of two codes out of thousands of possible ICD-9 codes.
  • primary_diagnosis_code is an ICD-9-CM code and that code set has thousands of very specific codes; here 717 of them occur.
  • ndc_code identifies a drug package: the same generic drug is sold under many labelers, strengths and package sizes, each with its own NDC (251 codes map to only 22 generic drugs, see Question 3); 125 of the 251 codes occur in fewer than 100 lines.
  • medical_specialty is a free list of 72 physician specialties (+ "?").

d. Demographics (one row per patient) - Age is skewed towards old patients: 66.6% of the patients are 60 or older, the mode is the 70-80 bucket (25.5%), followed by 60-70 (22.3%), 50-60 (17.4%) and 80-90 (16.2%); only 6.3% are younger than 40 and 0.2% younger than 10. The distribution is unimodal and left-skewed. Gender is nearly balanced with slightly more women: 53.2% female, 46.8% male, and 3 patients (<0.01%) with "Unknown/Invalid". The patient-level and line-level percentages are almost identical, so the denormalization does not distort these demographics.

Cutoff for the 5-7 day requirement. time_in_hospital is right-skewed (median 4, mean 4.4, max 14 days). 51.7% of the encounters last at least 4 days, 38.0% at least 5 days, 28.2% at least 6 and 20.8% at least 7. Because the drug needs at least 5-7 days in hospital, the lower end of that window, X = 5 days, is used as the cutoff: it keeps a pool of roughly four in ten patients, whereas 7 days would leave only about one in five and make the model's already limited precision matter more for a rare class. The same cutoff defines the "actual" label used in the evaluation (add_pred_to_test) and the prediction threshold in Question 10.

The optional TensorFlow Data Validation step was not used (the project notes say it has known visualization problems in recent browsers). The same analysis - missing/zero values, histograms and cardinality - is done above with pandas, seaborn/matplotlib and scipy.

Reduce Dimensionality of the NDC Code Feature¶

Question 3: NDC codes are a common format to represent the wide variety of drugs that are prescribed for patient care in the United States. The challenge is that there are many codes that map to the same or similar drug. You are provided with the ndc drug lookup file https://github.com/udacity/nd320-c1-emr-data-starter/blob/master/project/data_schema_references/ndc_lookup_table.csv derived from the National Drug Codes List site(https://ndclist.com/). Please use this file to come up with a way to reduce the dimensionality of this field and create a new field in the dataset called "generic_drug_name" in the output dataframe.

Select First Encounter for each Patient¶

Question 4: In order to simplify the aggregation of data for the model, we will only select the first encounter for each patient in the dataset. This is to reduce the risk of data leakage of future patient encounters and to reduce complexity of the data transformation and modeling steps. We will assume that sorting in numerical order on the encounter_id provides the time horizon for determining which encounters come before and after another.

Handling the "not measured" lab results first. max_glu_serum and A1Cresult hold "None" when the test was not taken (the data schema says so; newer pandas versions read that string as a missing value, older ones keep it as text). The next steps group on every non-drug column, and pandas.groupby silently drops rows with a missing group key, which would remove most encounters if the value is read as NaN. So the "not measured" level is made an explicit text value before aggregating, whichever pandas version is used.

In [18]:

first_encounter_df = select_first_encounter(reduce_dim_df)

Clinically Justified Cohort Filtering¶

Before aggregating, the first-encounter cohort is restricted to patients who could actually be enrolled in a trial of this drug. Each rule has a clinical rationale and is applied to the first encounter only (a patient whose first encounter is excluded is dropped entirely - we do not fall back to a later encounter, which would reintroduce the selection of "who comes back" and break the one-encounter-per-patient design):

rule clinical / data justification
Discharged expired or to hospice (discharge_disposition_id 11, 13, 14, 19, 20, 21) The stay was ended by death or a switch to palliative care, not by the treatment course, so the length of stay is truncated and says nothing about how long a trial patient would remain. These patients are also not eligible for a 5-7 day protocol with frequent testing and mobile-app adherence training.
Newborn admission / neonate discharge (admission_type_id 4, discharge_disposition_id 10) Neonatal care is not the adult diabetes population the drug is aimed at, and its stay length is driven by neonatal rather than diabetic factors.
Gender "Unknown/Invalid" An invalid demographic record (only 3 patients): it cannot be audited in the gender bias analysis and would produce a one-patient group.

The evidence cell below shows the effect: the 1,545 excluded expired/hospice first encounters (2.2% of patients) had a longer mean stay (5.0 days) than the others (4.3 days), so leaving them in would have made the pool of long-stay patients look larger than the pool that can really be enrolled.

Not filtered on purpose: patients who left against medical advice, transfers and short stays. These are exactly the cases a screening model must be able to recognise (a short expected stay means "exclude"). Filtering them out would make the model look better than it would behave in practice. The filter uses discharge_disposition_id, which is only known at the end of a stay; it defines who is in the retrospective study population and is not used as a model input (the model still sees discharge_disposition_id as a feature only in this retrospective setting - see the caveat in Question 5).

In [20]:
from student_utils import filter_eligible_encounters, add_diagnosis_group_features

# Evidence for the filters (first encounter of every patient, before filtering)
fe = first_encounter_df.drop_duplicates('encounter_id')
from student_utils import EXPIRED_OR_HOSPICE_DISCHARGE_IDS, NEONATE_DISCHARGE_IDS, NEWBORN_ADMISSION_TYPE_IDS
ids_map = pd.read_csv('../data_schema_references/IDs_mapping.csv') if os.path.exists('../data_schema_references/IDs_mapping.csv') else None
flag = fe['discharge_disposition_id'].isin(EXPIRED_OR_HOSPICE_DISCHARGE_IDS)
print("first encounters:", len(fe))
print("expired / hospice discharge: %d encounters (%.1f%%), mean stay %.2f days vs %.2f days for all others" %
      (flag.sum(), flag.mean() * 100, fe.loc[flag, 'time_in_hospital'].mean(), fe.loc[~flag, 'time_in_hospital'].mean()))
print("stay >= 5 days: %.1f%% of expired/hospice vs %.1f%% of the others" %
      ((fe.loc[flag, 'time_in_hospital'] >= 5).mean() * 100, (fe.loc[~flag, 'time_in_hospital'] >= 5).mean() * 100))
print("newborn admission type / neonate discharge:", int((fe['admission_type_id'].isin(NEWBORN_ADMISSION_TYPE_IDS) | fe['discharge_disposition_id'].isin(NEONATE_DISCHARGE_IDS)).sum()),
      "| gender Unknown/Invalid:", int((fe['gender'] == 'Unknown/Invalid').sum()))

Encounter-Level Representation of the Diagnoses (ICD-9 Grouping)¶

The dataset is at the line level (Question 1) and the model is at the encounter level, so every diagnosis field has to be turned into encounter-level features with a manageable dimensionality:

  • primary_diagnosis_code has 700+ distinct ICD-9 codes, and other_diagnosis_codes (two secondary codes in one string) has ~19,000 combinations. Used as raw categories they are sparse (most values occur a handful of times) and the second field is unusable.
  • Both are mapped to the ICD-9-CM chapters (circulatory, respiratory, digestive, injury, ...), with diabetes (250.xx) as its own group because it is the target condition. This gives primary_diagnosis_group and two secondary groups secondary_dx_group_1/2 with about 20 values each. The two secondary codes are an unordered pair in the source, so the groups are sorted alphabetically to give the same representation for ("diabetes", "circulatory") and ("circulatory", "diabetes").
  • The raw primary_diagnosis_code is kept as well, as a learned embedding, so the model can use the fine detail where it exists; the groups give it a dense, well-populated signal for the rare codes.
In [22]:

Aggregate Dataset to Right Level for Modeling¶

In order to provide a broad scope of the steps and to prevent students from getting stuck with data transformations, we have selected the aggregation columns and provided a function to build the dataset at the appropriate level. The 'aggregate_dataset" function that you can find in the 'utils.py' file can take the preceding dataframe with the 'generic_drug_name' field and transform the data appropriately for the project.

To make it simpler for students, we are creating dummy columns for each unique generic drug name and adding those are input features to the model. There are other options for data representation but this is out of scope for the time constraints of the course.

Student response:

weight - EXCLUDE. 96.9% of the encounters have no weight (only 3,197 of 101,766 have a value) and the recorded ones are spread over 9 coarse bins. A feature that is missing for almost everyone cannot be learned reliably, and imputing it would essentially invent the feature.

payer_code - EXCLUDE. 39.6% of the encounters have no payer ("?"), and the rest is spread over 17 payers of which 8 have fewer than 1% of the encounters each. Among the 10 payer groups with at least 1,000 encounters the mean stay only ranges from 3.69 to 4.59 days (0.90 days, compared with a standard deviation of a stay of 2.99 days), and the "missing" group (4.59 days) is not distinct enough to be informative. Payer is an administrative/financial attribute and a proxy for insurance status and socio-economic background rather than a clinical driver of the length of stay, so it adds little signal while adding a bias risk for a model that decides who is offered a trial.

Other choices. Categorical: admission type, discharge disposition, admission source, the primary diagnosis (raw ICD-9 code, embedded because of its high cardinality) plus the ICD-9 groups of the primary diagnosis and of the two secondary diagnoses (primary_diagnosis_group, secondary_dx_group_1/2, see the ICD grouping section), max_glu_serum, A1Cresult, change, the three required demographics (race, gender, age) and the 22 drug indicator columns from the aggregation. Age is a categorical 10-year band, and a crossed feature of age x admission type is added in the TF feature columns. Numerical: num_lab_procedures, num_medications, number_diagnoses, num_procedures. Excluded: readmitted (an outcome after discharge - it would leak future information), the raw other_diagnosis_codes (15,494 combinations - represented by the two ICD groups instead), medical_specialty (49% missing), the prior-visit counts number_outpatient/inpatient/emergency (67-89% zeros and extreme skew), and the IDs. Caveat: some of the kept fields (num_lab_procedures, num_medications, discharge_disposition_id) are only final at the end of a stay; they make this a retrospective analysis of the dataset and would need to be replaced by admission-time information before the model is used to screen patients at admission.

def select_model_features(df, categorical_col_list, numerical_col_list, PREDICTOR_FIELD, grouping_key='patient_nbr'):
    selected_col_list = [grouping_key] + [PREDICTOR_FIELD] + categorical_col_list + numerical_col_list   
    return agg_drug_df[selected_col_list]

Preprocess Dataset - Casting and Imputing¶

We will cast and impute the dataset before splitting so that we do not have to repeat these steps across the splits in the next step. For imputing, there can be deeper analysis into which features to impute and how to impute but for the sake of time, we are taking a general strategy of imputing zero for only numerical features.

Split Dataset into Train, Validation, and Test Partitions¶

Question 6: In order to prepare the data for being trained and evaluated by a deep learning model, we will split the dataset into three partitions, with the validation partition used for optimizing the model hyperparameters during training. One of the key parts is that we need to be sure that the data does not accidently leak across partitions.

Please complete the function below to split the input dataset into three partitions(train, validation, test) with the following requirements.

  • Approximately 60%/20%/20% train/validation/test split
  • Randomly sample different patients into each data partition
  • IMPORTANT Make sure that a patient's data is not in more than one partition, so that we can avoid possible data leakage.
  • Make sure that the total number of unique patients across the splits is equal to the total number of unique patients in the original dataset
  • Total number of rows in original dataset = sum of rows across all three dataset partitions

def partition_profile(col):
    parts = {'full': processed_df.drop_duplicates('patient_nbr'), 'train': d_train, 'validation': d_val, 'test': d_test}
    return pd.concat({k: v[col].value_counts(normalize=True) * 100 for k, v in parts.items()}, axis=1).round(1)

4. Create Categorical Features with TF Feature Columns¶

Build Vocabulary for Categorical Features¶

Before we can create the TF categorical features, we must first create the vocab files with the unique values for a given field that are from the training dataset. Below we have provided a function that you can use that only requires providing the pandas train dataset partition and the list of the categorical columns in a list format. The output variable 'vocab_file_list' will be a list of the file paths that can be used in the next step for creating the categorical features.

Dimensionality of the categorical features. create_tf_categorical_feature_cols one-hot encodes (indicator column) every field with a small vocabulary and uses a learned embedding for fields with more than 50 values - here primary_diagnosis_code (ICD-9, 700+ values) - so one high-cardinality code set does not add hundreds of sparse columns.

Cross feature (extra). Older patients admitted through an emergency behave differently from younger elective admissions, which a model of single columns can only learn indirectly. A crossed feature column gives the model the age-band x admission-type combination directly.

5. Create Numerical Features with TF Feature Columns¶

Question 8: Using the TF Feature Column API(https://www.tensorflow.org/api_docs/python/tf/feature_column/), please create normalized Tensorflow numeric features for the model. Try to use the z-score normalizer function below to help as well as the 'calculate_stats_from_train_data' function.

In [48]:
from student_utils import create_tf_numeric_feature

For simplicity the create_tf_numerical_feature_cols function below uses the same normalizer function across all features(z-score normalization) but if you have time feel free to analyze and adapt the normalizer based off the statistical distributions. You may find this as a good resource in determining which transformation fits best for the data https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/data-prep/transform/normalization.

In [49]:
def calculate_stats_from_train_data(df, col):
    mean = df[col].describe()['mean']
    std = df[col].describe()['std']
    return mean, std

def create_tf_numerical_feature_cols(numerical_col_list, train_df):
    tf_numeric_col_list = []
    for c in numerical_col_list:
        mean, std = calculate_stats_from_train_data(train_df, c)
        tf_numeric_feature = create_tf_numeric_feature(c, mean, std)
        tf_numeric_col_list.append(tf_numeric_feature)
    return tf_numeric_col_list

6. Build Deep Learning Regression Model with Sequential API and TF Probability Layers¶

Use DenseFeatures to combine features for model¶

Now that we have prepared categorical and numerical features using Tensorflow's Feature Column API, we can combine them into a dense vector representation for the model. Below we will create this new input layer, which we will call 'claim_feature_layer'.

In [54]:
claim_feature_columns = tf_cat_col_list + tf_cont_col_list + tf_cross_col_list
claim_feature_layer = tf.keras.layers.DenseFeatures(claim_feature_columns)

Build Sequential API Model from DenseFeatures and TF Probability Layers¶

Below we have provided some boilerplate code for building a model that connects the Sequential API, DenseFeatures, and Tensorflow Probability layers into a deep learning model. There are many opportunities to further optimize and explore different architectures through benchmarking and testing approaches in various research papers, loss and evaluation metrics, learning curves, hyperparameter tuning, TF probability layers, etc. Feel free to modify and explore as you wish.

OPTIONAL: Come up with a more optimal neural network architecture and hyperparameters. Share the process in discovering the architecture and hyperparameters.

In [55]:
def build_sequential_model(feature_layer):
    model = tf.keras.Sequential([
        feature_layer,
        tf.keras.layers.Dense(150, activation='relu'),
        tf.keras.layers.Dense(75, activation='relu'),
        tfp.layers.DenseVariational(1+1, posterior_mean_field, prior_trainable),
        tfp.layers.DistributionLambda(
            lambda t:tfp.distributions.Normal(loc=t[..., :1],
                                             scale=1e-3 + tf.math.softplus(0.01 * t[...,1:])
                                             )
        ),
    ])
    return model

def build_diabetes_model(train_ds, val_ds,  feature_layer,  epochs=5, loss_metric='mse'):
    model = build_sequential_model(feature_layer)
    model.compile(optimizer='rmsprop', loss=loss_metric, metrics=[loss_metric])
    early_stop = tf.keras.callbacks.EarlyStopping(monitor=loss_metric, patience=3)     
    history = model.fit(train_ds, validation_data=val_ds,
                        callbacks=[early_stop],
                        epochs=epochs)
    return model, history

def plot_learning_curves(h, train_key, val_key, title, ylabel):
    plt.figure(figsize=(7, 4))
    plt.plot(h.history[train_key], label='train'); plt.plot(h.history[val_key], label='validation')
    plt.xlabel('epoch'); plt.ylabel(ylabel); plt.title(title); plt.legend(); plt.show()

Optional: a better architecture for uncertainty (heteroscedastic Normal output)¶

The provided model keeps the standard deviation almost constant: it is trained with MSE only, and the scale is softplus(0.01 * t), so its gradient is scaled down 100x and the loss never rewards a good uncertainty estimate. A prediction interval that has the same width for every patient cannot be used to rank patients. Process followed to improve it:

  1. Loss - train the mean and the scale together with the negative log-likelihood of the Normal distribution (-p_y.log_prob(y)), the proper scoring rule for a probabilistic output.
  2. Output head - a plain Dense(2) that feeds tfp.distributions.Normal(loc, scale). I first kept the DenseVariational head with NLL (also with the KL term re-weighted by 1/N and several learning rates) but it trained unstably - the stochastic weights add noise to both the mean and the scale - and its validation NLL stayed worse than predicting a constant.
  3. Initialisation - the output bias starts at the training mean and the inverse softplus of the training std so that optimisation starts from the marginal distribution instead of from 0.
  4. Regularisation - without it the model overfits after 2 epochs (training loss keeps falling while validation loss stops improving), so L2 (1e-4) and dropout (0.3) are added.
  5. Optimiser / stopping - Adam (1e-3) with early stopping on the validation loss and restoring the best weights.

The two models are then compared on the validation set (the test set is only used for the final evaluation).

In [58]:
def nll_loss(y_true, p_y):
    # negative log-likelihood of the label under the predicted Normal distribution
    return -p_y.log_prob(y_true)

def build_heteroscedastic_model(feature_layer, y_mean, y_std):
    scale_bias_init = float(np.log(np.expm1(y_std)))      # inverse softplus -> initial scale = training std
    return tf.keras.Sequential([
        feature_layer,
        tf.keras.layers.Dense(150, activation='relu', kernel_regularizer=tf.keras.regularizers.l2(1e-4)),
        tf.keras.layers.Dropout(0.3),
        tf.keras.layers.Dense(75, activation='relu', kernel_regularizer=tf.keras.regularizers.l2(1e-4)),
        tf.keras.layers.Dropout(0.3),
        tf.keras.layers.Dense(1 + 1, bias_initializer=tf.keras.initializers.Constant([float(y_mean), scale_bias_init])),
        tfp.layers.DistributionLambda(
            lambda t: tfp.distributions.Normal(loc=t[..., :1], scale=1e-3 + tf.math.softplus(t[..., 1:]))),
    ])

def build_tuned_model(train_ds, val_ds, feature_layer, y_mean, y_std, epochs=40):
    model = build_heteroscedastic_model(feature_layer, y_mean, y_std)
    model.compile(optimizer=tf.keras.optimizers.Adam(1e-3), loss=nll_loss)
    early_stop = tf.keras.callbacks.EarlyStopping(monitor='val_loss', patience=5, restore_best_weights=True)
    hist = model.fit(train_ds, validation_data=val_ds, callbacks=[early_stop], epochs=epochs, verbose=2)
    return model, hist

set_seeds(42)
tuned_model, tuned_history = build_tuned_model(diabetes_train_ds, diabetes_val_ds, claim_feature_layer,
                                               d_train[PREDICTOR_FIELD].mean(), d_train[PREDICTOR_FIELD].std())

In [60]:
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score, mean_squared_error, mean_absolute_error
feature_list = student_categorical_col_list + student_numerical_col_list

def regression_report(model, split_df):
    yhat = model(dict(split_df[feature_list]))
    mean, std = yhat.mean().numpy().flatten(), yhat.stddev().numpy().flatten()
    y = split_df[PREDICTOR_FIELD].values
    return {'RMSE (days)': mean_squared_error(y, mean) ** 0.5, 'MAE (days)': mean_absolute_error(y, mean),
            'AUC of mean vs. stay>=5': roc_auc_score(y >= 5, mean), 'std min': std.min(), 'std max': std.max(),
            'corr(std, |error|)': np.corrcoef(std, np.abs(mean - y))[0, 1]}

y_val = d_val[PREDICTOR_FIELD].values
val_reports = {'baseline': regression_report(baseline_model, d_val), 'tuned': regression_report(tuned_model, d_val)}
comparison = pd.DataFrame({'baseline (provided TFP model)': val_reports['baseline'],
                           'tuned (heteroscedastic NLL)': val_reports['tuned']}).T
comparison.loc['predict the training mean', ['RMSE (days)', 'MAE (days)']] = [
    mean_squared_error(y_val, np.full_like(y_val, d_train[PREDICTOR_FIELD].mean(), dtype=float)) ** 0.5,
    mean_absolute_error(y_val, np.full_like(y_val, d_train[PREDICTOR_FIELD].mean(), dtype=float))]
print("VALIDATION set:")
comparison.round(3)

Uncertainty estimates: prediction intervals, calibration and ranking¶

pred_mean is the expected number of days and pred_std the model's uncertainty. Below, (1) a 95% interval mean ± 1.96 std is built and its calibration checked on the test set, (2) each patient gets the probability of meeting the stay requirement under the predicted Normal distribution, and (3) the patients the model selects are ranked by that probability so the company can start with the ones it is most sure about.

In [66]:
from scipy.stats import norm
from student_utils import CUTOFF_DAYS

prob_output_df['lower_95'] = prob_output_df['pred_mean'] - 1.96 * prob_output_df['pred_std']
prob_output_df['upper_95'] = prob_output_df['pred_mean'] + 1.96 * prob_output_df['pred_std']
inside = ((prob_output_df['actual_value'] >= prob_output_df['lower_95']) & (prob_output_df['actual_value'] <= prob_output_df['upper_95'])).mean()
print("share of actual stays inside the 95%% interval: %.1f%% (a calibrated model gives ~95%%)" % (inside * 100))
print("pred_std: min %.2f | median %.2f | max %.2f days" % (prob_output_df['pred_std'].min(), prob_output_df['pred_std'].median(), prob_output_df['pred_std'].max()))

# stays are whole days, so "at least CUTOFF_DAYS days" is P(X >= CUTOFF_DAYS - 0.5) for the continuous Normal
prob_output_df['p_meets_cutoff'] = 1 - norm.cdf(CUTOFF_DAYS - 0.5, loc=prob_output_df['pred_mean'], scale=prob_output_df['pred_std'])
prob_output_df['actually_meets_cutoff'] = (prob_output_df['actual_value'] >= CUTOFF_DAYS).astype(int)

selected = prob_output_df[prob_output_df['pred_mean'] >= CUTOFF_DAYS].copy()
selected['confidence_tier'] = pd.qcut(selected['p_meets_cutoff'], 3, labels=['3 - lower confidence', '2 - medium confidence', '1 - highest confidence'])
tiers = (selected.groupby('confidence_tier', observed=True)
         .agg(patients=('pred_mean', 'size'), avg_pred_mean=('pred_mean', 'mean'), avg_pred_std=('pred_std', 'mean'),
              share_that_really_stayed_long_enough=('actually_meets_cutoff', 'mean')).sort_index())
print("\nPatients the model would select (pred_mean >= %d days), ranked in three tiers by P(stay >= %d days):" % (CUTOFF_DAYS, CUTOFF_DAYS))
tiers.round(3)

Convert Regression Output to Classification Output for Patient Selection¶

Question 10: Given the output predictions, convert it to a binary label for whether the patient meets the time criteria or does not (HINT: use the mean prediction numpy array). The expected output is a numpy array with a 1 or 0 based off if the prediction meets or doesnt meet the criteria.

In [68]:
from student_utils import get_student_binary_prediction
student_binary_prediction = get_student_binary_prediction(prob_output_df, 'pred_mean')

Cutoff used. The drug has to be given for at least 5-7 days in hospital. From the distribution in the EDA (38.0% of the encounters last >= 5 days, 20.8% >= 7 days), the cutoff is 5 days, the start of that window. A patient is selected (1) if the model's expected stay (pred_mean) is >= 5 days and excluded (0) otherwise. This is the same threshold add_pred_to_test uses to create the actual label (time_in_hospital >= 5), so the prediction and the label are defined consistently; it is stored as CUTOFF_DAYS in student_utils.py.

In [69]:
print("selected for the trial:", int(student_binary_prediction.sum()), "of", len(student_binary_prediction),
      "test patients (%.1f%%)" % (student_binary_prediction.mean() * 100))
print("unique values:", np.unique(student_binary_prediction))

Output Prediction Dataset¶

The table below is the output prediction dataset for the test set (one row per test patient, in the order of d_test). It combines the TF Probability outputs - pred_mean (expected days) and pred_std (uncertainty) - with the binary prediction (binary_prediction: 1 = include in the trial because the expected stay is at least 5 days, 0 = exclude) and the binary actual value (binary_actual: 1 = the patient really stayed at least 5 days) derived from actual_value. It is saved as prob_output_df_final.csv.

In [70]:
# Output prediction dataset: regression outputs (mean, std) + the binary prediction and the binary actual value
prob_output_df['binary_prediction'] = student_binary_prediction                                   # 1 = include in trial, 0 = exclude
prob_output_df['binary_actual'] = (prob_output_df['actual_value'] >= CUTOFF_DAYS).astype(int)    # 1 = really stayed >= cutoff days
prob_output_df.insert(0, 'patient_nbr', d_test['patient_nbr'].values)                            # rows are in d_test order, so the ids line up
assert (prob_output_df['actual_value'].values == d_test['time_in_hospital'].values).all()
prob_output_df.to_csv('prob_output_df_final.csv', index=False)
print("saved prob_output_df_final.csv:", prob_output_df.shape)

Add Binary Prediction to Test Dataframe¶

Using the student_binary_prediction output that is a numpy array with binary labels, we can use this to add to a dataframe to better visualize and also to prepare the data for the Aequitas toolkit. The Aequitas toolkit requires that the predictions be mapped to a binary label for the predictions (called 'score' field) and the actual value (called 'label_value').

In [71]:
def add_pred_to_test(test_df, pred_np, demo_col_list):
    for c in demo_col_list:
        test_df[c] = test_df[c].astype(str)
    test_df['score'] = pred_np
    test_df['label_value'] = test_df['time_in_hospital'].apply(lambda x: 1 if x >=5 else 0)
    return test_df

pred_test_df = add_pred_to_test(d_test, student_binary_prediction, ['race', 'gender'])

Model Evaluation Metrics¶

Question 11: Now it is time to use the newly created binary labels in the 'pred_test_df' dataframe to evaluate the model with some common classification metrics. Please create a report summary of the performance of the model and be sure to give the ROC AUC, F1 score(weighted), class precision and recall scores.

For the report please be sure to include the following three parts:

  • With a non-technical audience in mind, explain the precision-recall tradeoff in regard to how you have optimized your model.

  • What are some areas of improvement for future iterations?

In [73]:
# AUC, F1, precision and recall
from sklearn.metrics import (roc_auc_score, f1_score, precision_score, recall_score, accuracy_score,
                             classification_report, confusion_matrix, ConfusionMatrixDisplay)

y_true = pred_test_df['label_value']
y_pred = pred_test_df['score']

print("ROC AUC (binary selection decision):   %.3f" % roc_auc_score(y_true, y_pred))
print("ROC AUC (using pred_mean as the score): %.3f" % roc_auc_score(y_true, prob_output_df['pred_mean']))
print("F1 (weighted):                          %.3f" % f1_score(y_true, y_pred, average='weighted'))
print("Accuracy:                               %.3f" % accuracy_score(y_true, y_pred))
print()
print(classification_report(y_true, y_pred, target_names=['stay < %d days (exclude)' % CUTOFF_DAYS, 'stay >= %d days (include)' % CUTOFF_DAYS], digits=3))

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 4.8))
ConfusionMatrixDisplay(confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred), display_labels=['exclude', 'include']).plot(ax=axes[0], colorbar=False, cmap='Blues')
axes[0].set_title('Confusion matrix (test set)')
# precision/recall as the selection cutoff on the predicted number of days moves
thr = np.arange(3, 8.01, 0.25)
pr = pd.DataFrame({'cutoff on predicted days': thr,
                   'precision': [precision_score(y_true, prob_output_df['pred_mean'] >= t, zero_division=0) for t in thr],
                   'recall': [recall_score(y_true, prob_output_df['pred_mean'] >= t) for t in thr],
                   'patients selected': [(prob_output_df['pred_mean'] >= t).sum() for t in thr]}).set_index('cutoff on predicted days')
pr[['precision', 'recall']].plot(ax=axes[1], marker='o'); axes[1].axvline(CUTOFF_DAYS, c='k', ls='--', lw=1)
axes[1].set_title('Precision-recall trade-off when moving the selection cutoff'); axes[1].set_ylabel('score'); axes[1].grid(alpha=.3)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
pr.loc[[3.5, 4.0, 4.5, 5.0, 5.5, 6.0, 7.0]].round(3)

The regression model itself reduces the validation RMSE from 2.92 days (always predicting the average stay) to 2.12 days, and its 95% prediction interval contains 95.0% of the real stays on the test set (well calibrated).

1. Precision-recall trade-off for a non-technical audience. Precision answers "of the patients we pick for the trial, how many really stay long enough?" (73%: about 3 of 4). Recall answers "of all the patients who would stay long enough, how many do we find?" (63%). They pull in opposite directions: if we only pick patients the model is very sure about (a higher cutoff on the predicted stay, 7 days instead of 5) almost everybody we pick is right (precision 92%) but we overlook most eligible patients (recall 24%); if we are generous (cutoff 4 days) we find 82% of the eligible patients but 38% of those we enrolled leave too early, and each of those costs extra monitoring and training. Because every wrongly enrolled patient is expensive for the study, I kept the cutoff at 5 days, which matches the clinical requirement and gives a reasonable balance (the plot above shows the whole trade-off, so the company can move the cutoff if the cost of a missed patient or a wasted slot changes). The uncertainty estimate adds a second lever: ranking the selected patients by the probability of meeting the requirement gives a "highest confidence" third of which 91% really stayed >= 5 days, versus 56% for the "lower confidence" third - so enrolment can start with the safest patients.

2. Areas of improvement. (a) Use only information that is known at admission (see Question 5) so the model can screen patients before the stay; (b) richer diagnosis features: the ICD-9 chapter groups are used now, but finer clinical groupings (e.g. CCS categories), pre-trained code embeddings or a conditional-probability matrix of diagnosis pairs could add signal, and the prior-visit history could be added with a log transform; (c) tune/ensemble the network (depth, embedding size, learning rate, class weights) and compare with a gradient-boosted baseline; (d) model the full patient history (longitudinal) instead of only the first encounter; (e) predict the probability of staying >= 5 days directly or with a distribution that fits the skewed counts better (Poisson/negative binomial) instead of a Normal, which allows negative stays; (f) better imputation than zeros and more data for under-represented groups (see the bias analysis).

3. Bias-variance trade-off. The first (provided) TFP model has a modest gap between training and validation error (MSE 5.92 vs 6.47 at the last epoch) - it is not overfit - but its error is still larger than the tuned model's and its uncertainty is nearly meaningless (a standard deviation of 0.70 for everybody), so its main limitation is bias (a too noisy output layer and an uncertainty that is not trained) plus the limited information in the features: a length of stay is inherently noisy. The more flexible heteroscedastic network without regularisation went the other way: in my trials its training loss kept falling while the validation loss stopped improving after about 2 epochs (variance/overfitting). L2 regularisation, dropout and early stopping on the validation loss moved it to a good middle: the final training and validation negative log-likelihood are close (2.04 vs 2.09, against about 2.50 for a constant prediction), the validation RMSE is lower than the baseline's (2.12 vs 2.17) and the intervals are calibrated. The remaining error is mostly irreducible noise and missing information, not model variance, so more capacity would help little compared with better features. For this problem the cost of variance is high because a model that memorises the training patients would pick patients who then leave early; this is why the patients are split by patient and the model is chosen on validation data only.

7. Evaluating Potential Model Biases with Aequitas Toolkit¶

Prepare Data For Aequitas Bias Toolkit¶

Using the gender and race fields, we will prepare the data for the Aequitas Toolkit.

In [74]:
# Aequitas
from aequitas.preprocessing import preprocess_input_df
from aequitas.group import Group
from aequitas.plotting import Plot
from aequitas.bias import Bias
from aequitas.fairness import Fairness

ae_subset_df = pred_test_df[['race', 'gender', 'score', 'label_value']]
ae_df, _ = preprocess_input_df(ae_subset_df)
g = Group()
xtab, _ = g.get_crosstabs(ae_df)
absolute_metrics = g.list_absolute_metrics(xtab)
clean_xtab = xtab.fillna(-1)
aqp = Plot()
b = Bias()

Race and Gender Bias Analysis for Patient Selection¶

for metric in ['fdr_disparity', 'tpr_disparity']:

Student Response. Two metrics matter for selection: FDR (of the patients we select, the share that will not stay long enough - wasted enrolment and extra cost for the company) and TPR / recall (of the patients who would qualify, the share the model finds - who gets the chance to take part). The plots above use the groups of race and gender. The invalid-gender record was already removed in the cohort filtering, so every plotted group has a meaningful size; the smallest race groups (Asian 86, Other 232, Hispanic 296 test patients) are noisy.

  • Gender: no bias. TPR is 0.632 for women and 0.626 for men, and FDR is 0.273 for both (disparities 1.01 and 1.00).
  • Race, TPR: no group is outside the fairness band. African American 0.649, Caucasian (reference) 0.629, Asian 0.632, Other 0.605, Hispanic 0.558 (disparity 0.89) and unknown race "?" 0.561 (0.89). The two lowest groups are small and, although inside the 0.8-1.25 band, they find about 6-7 points fewer of their qualifying patients than the reference.
  • Race, FDR: one group is outside the band. The patients whose race is unknown ("?", 372 test patients) have an FDR of 0.340 vs 0.265 for the reference (disparity 1.28 > 1.25): a third of the "?" patients the model selects will not stay long enough. All other groups are within the band (African American 0.294, Asian 0.294, Other 0.292, Hispanic 0.264).

Conclusion: there is no significant bias by gender, and the model finds qualifying patients at a similar rate across the recorded race groups. The one flagged result is the missing-race group, which is a data-quality group and not a demographic group of patients, so it needs a look at how race is recorded rather than a conclusion about a population. Because the smallest groups have only 86-372 test patients, their metrics can move a lot from one training run to the next, so differences of this size should be re-checked with confidence intervals before they are acted on.

Fairness Analysis Example - Relative to a Reference Group¶

Student Response. The reference groups are Caucasian (race) and Male (gender), the largest groups. Aequitas divides each group's metric by the reference group's metric (the disparity) and marks a group as fair when the ratio is within 0.8-1.25. The plots above show this for TPR and FDR.

  • TPR (equal opportunity): every group is "fair" (all green in the fairness plot). Disparities relative to Caucasian patients: African American 1.03, Asian 1.01, Other 0.96, Hispanic 0.89, unknown race 0.89; Female vs Male 1.01. The model therefore identifies qualifying patients at a similar rate across the groups, and the lowest groups (Hispanic, unknown race) are the ones to watch because they are about 11% below the reference and small.
  • FDR (cost of wrongly selected patients): the unknown-race group "?" is the only one outside the band (disparity 1.28, "FDR Parity" = False): a selected patient of unknown race is more likely to be a wasted slot than a selected Caucasian patient (34% vs 27%). The other groups are within the band (African American 1.11, Asian 1.11, Other 1.10, Hispanic 0.99, Female 1.00).

Interpretation and caveats: The only disparity flagged is for a group of 372 test patients whose race was not recorded, so it may reflect differences in the case mix or in the data capture at the hospitals that do not record race, and the 372 patients make it a noisy estimate (no significance test was run). For the recorded groups the model is within the fairness band for both metrics. Suggested follow-up: investigate how race is recorded (and whether it correlates with site), report confidence intervals (bootstrap or Aequitas' significance test), collect more data for the small groups (Asian, Other, Hispanic make up under 5% of patients) and re-run this analysis whenever the model changes.
